newsitem.title: USA: Dismal Bristol Bay salmon run puzzles officials.
newsitem.headline: Dismal Bristol Bay salmon run puzzles officials.

text.p: An unexpectedly dismal return of sockeye salmon to southwestern Alaska's Bristol Bay is likely to produce the smallest harvest there since 1988, a state official said on Monday.

Weak runs into some of the region's districts have caused the Alaska Department of Fish and Game to halve its pre-season forecast of a 25 million sockeye harvest on a 30 million fish return, spokesman Herman Savikko said.

So far, only 10.8 million sockeye salmon have been netted in the Bristol Bay region on a run of 16.4 million fish, Savikko said. By summer's end, the department expects a harvest of no more than 15 million fish on a run of 20 million, he said.
"Compare it to that record (harvest) that we had just a few years ago, of 44 million, it certainly pales," he said.
This year's return may signal a reversion to the relatively small harvests of the late 1980s, he said.
Bristol Bay is the site of the world's largest natural sockeye run, with total returns to the area's rivers and streams topping 40 million in recent years and harvests above 30 million fish.
The reason for this year's weak return is unclear, Savikko said.
"It doesn't appear to be a problem of freshwater survival. It appears to be something in the marine waters that's affecting them," he said.
The low harvest has not yet produced a rise in prices for Alaska salmon, Savikko said.

"When you have a partial failure like we have here, normally you would expect prices to jump up around the state. But as of yet that hasn't happened," he said. "If they don't jump, I think that's even spookier, because that indicates there's not enough interest in the product."
Prices for Bristol Bay sockeye salmon have ranged from 50 cents to 80 cents a pound this year, compared with the nearly $3 a pound fetched in 1988.
Savikko said other sockeye returns in southwestern Alaska had been weaker than expected.

Even with an anticipated record return of Copper River sockeye near Prince William Sound, "there's going to be a 12-plus million shortage anyway, and you certainly would think that that would have price impacts," he said.
Gov. Tony Knowles and Lt. Gov. Fran Ulmer, both Democrats, traveled to the Bristol Bay region over the weekend to hear the complaints of affected fishermen.
And U.S. Sen. Frank Murkowski said on Monday he had asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Small Business Administration to prepare disaster declarations for the region.

"For the thousands of independent fishing captains, crew members and processing workers affected by this failure, many of whom are residents of local villages with few other resource, this is a disater of the first order that will have an extreme impact," the Republican senator said in a news release.
